questions.q: completeTask saves the task, then sends an email, updates statistics and clears the cache itself. What is the main problem?
questions.explain: The parts are tied together, so a change in one forces changes in the others. With events, completeTask only saves and announces; each reaction lives in its own handler.
options: It is too slow to run
It is coupled: every new reaction to a finished task means editing this function, and a failing mailer makes the saved task look failed
It cannot be tested at all
JavaScript cannot call four functions in a row

questions.q: Which is the best name for an event?
questions.explain: An event says "this happened", in the past tense, as namespace.action in lowercase words joined by dots. sendWelcomeEmail is an order to do something, not an event.
options: sendWelcomeEmail
complete.task
task.completed
TaskCompleteNow

questions.q: What does the code that publishes task.completed know about the handlers?
questions.explain: That is the point of events: the publisher does its job and announces it. Publishing to nobody is not an error.
options: It must know every handler, to call them in the right order
Nothing: it does not know who is listening, or whether anyone is
It knows how many handlers there are and fails if there are none
It must import every handler file

questions.q: What is the event bus?
questions.explain: Publishers hand events to the bus, and the bus calls every matching handler. This bus lives in the memory of one process.
options: A database table that stores every event forever
The object in the middle that keeps the list of handlers and delivers each event to them
A network connection between two servers
A queue that retries failed events

questions.q: Why are events frozen, so nobody can change them after they were created?
questions.explain: A frozen event is the same for every handler. If a handler needs changed data, it copies the payload first.
options: To save memory
So they can be sent over the network
Many handlers see the same event; if one could change the payload, the next handler would see different data depending on the order
Because JavaScript objects are always frozen

questions.q: A developer calls bus.on("task.completed", ...) inside a request handler. What goes wrong?
questions.explain: This is a listener leak. Subscribe your handlers once, when the app starts. The bus warns you when one event type collects more than 100 handlers.
options: Nothing, the bus removes old handlers automatically
The handler never runs
Every request adds another copy, so each event runs the handler more and more times and memory grows forever
The request fails with an error

questions.q: Three handlers match an event: priority 10, priority 0 and priority -10. In which order do they run?
questions.explain: Higher numbers run first, and the default is 0. Handlers with the same priority run in the order they subscribed. An audit log at -10 always runs last.
options: -10, 0, 10
10, 0, -10
In the order they subscribed, whatever the priority
In a random order

questions.q: Handler B only works if handler A ran first. What does the lesson suggest?
questions.explain: Use priorities sparingly. Two handlers that depend on each other's order are really one job, so keep them together.
options: Give B a higher priority than A
Use parallel mode so they run together
They are not really independent: consider doing both in one handler
Subscribe B twice to be sure

questions.q: Three handlers each call a different outside API and take about 300 ms. Which dispatch mode fits best?
questions.explain: Parallel mode starts all handlers at once and waits for the slowest. Use sequential when order matters or handlers share something, like one database connection.
options: Sequential, because it is the default
Parallel: they are independent, so the publish takes about 300 ms instead of 900 ms
Sequential with priorities, so the fastest runs first
It makes no difference

questions.q: The email handler throws because the mail server is down. The task was already saved. What does the bus do by default?
questions.explain: Failing the request would be wrong, because the task was saved. So the other handlers still run, and each failure is reported in result.errors and to the onError hook.
options: It stops and rejects the publish, so the request fails
It retries the email handler until it works
It runs the other handlers anyway and reports the failure in the result (the CONTINUE mode)
It ignores the error completely

questions.q: Why should the Task API log handler failures in the bus's onError hook?
questions.explain: onError sees every failure once the handlers have run, even when the publisher ignores the result. Log it there with the logger.
options: Because result.errors is always empty
An error that is only in a result nobody reads is an error nobody will ever see
Because onError retries the handler
Because onError stops other handlers from running

questions.q: When is the THROW error mode a good choice?
questions.explain: In THROW mode the first failing handler rejects the publish and the handlers after it do not run. That is useful when any failure must stop you, like in a test.
options: In production, so emails are never lost
When every handler must succeed, for example in a test
When handlers are slow
When nobody listens to the event

questions.q: You write a middleware with bus.use(async (context, next) => { ... }). What must it do with next()?
questions.explain: next() runs the rest: other middleware, then the handlers. Returning without calling it stops the event (shortCircuited: true); forgetting to return its result hides what the handlers did.
options: Call it twice, before and after logging
Await it and return its result, or the bus cannot see what the handlers did
Never call it; the bus calls the handlers itself
Call it without await so it runs in the background

questions.q: The lesson adds bus.use(validateEventMiddleware(check, { priority: 100 })). Why priority 100?
questions.explain: The outermost middleware runs first. A validation check belongs there, so an invalid event is rejected before any other code touches it. bus.use accepts the ready-made middleware directly, as does the middleware option of createEventBus.
options: So it runs after the handlers
It becomes the outermost layer, so a bad event never reaches the logging or the handlers
Because middleware without a priority is ignored
So it runs in parallel with the handlers

questions.q: Linus tries to complete Ada's task. Where does the ownership check belong?
questions.explain: If the event were published, the email, statistics and cache handlers would all react to something Linus was not allowed to do. Check permissions first, then publish.
options: In each handler, after the event is published
In the service, before publishing: once an event is out, every handler trusts it
In an event middleware only
Nowhere, events are only for logging

questions.q: The process crashes after the task was saved but before the email handler ran. What happens to the email?
questions.explain: This bus keeps events only in memory, and nothing retries them. For work that must happen, put a job on a queue (the background jobs lesson).
options: The bus retries it when the process restarts
It is never sent: in-memory events can be lost, so work that must happen belongs on a queue
Another server picks it up
The task save is rolled back

questions.q: Why should you publish task.completed after the database transaction commits?
questions.explain: Handlers react at once: an email could go out for a task that was never saved. Publish once the data is really saved.
options: Because publishing inside a transaction is slower
If the transaction rolls back, handlers would already have reacted to something that never happened
Because the bus cannot run while a transaction is open
Because events must be stored in the database first

questions.q: You run two copies of the Task API. Copy A publishes task.completed. Do handlers in copy B run?
questions.explain: This bus lives in the memory of one process. Another copy has its own bus and never hears about the event.
options: Yes, the bus sends events to every copy
No, each copy has its own bus; events between services need a message broker
Only if both copies use the same port
Only for wildcard handlers

questions.q: Subscribe a handler to task.completed that prints email to <userId>: well done on "<title>" from the payload. Then publish one event for Ada with the title Buy milk.
questions.explain: bus.on(type, handler) subscribes. bus.publishEvent({ type, payload }) calls every matching handler and resolves with a result once they have all finished.
questions.expected:
email to ada: well done on "Buy milk"
handlers: 1

questions.q: Create a typed definition TaskCompletedEvent with defineEvent for the type task.completed and the TaskCompleted payload. The handler and the publish lines are already written.
questions.explain: defineEvent<"task.completed", TaskCompleted>("task.completed") knows the name and the payload type, so create checks the payload and no file can mistype the event name.

questions.q: Subscribe email with bus.on so it prints email #<taskId>, and a badge handler with bus.once that prints badge. After the second publish, unsubscribe the email handler.
questions.explain: bus.on returns a subscription; keep it to call unsubscribe() later. bus.once removes itself after the first event.

questions.q: Subscribe one handler to task.* that counts events per type in the counts map.
questions.explain: task.* matches every event in the task namespace but not user.registered. event.type tells the handler which one arrived.

questions.q: Three handlers are subscribed in the wrong order. Add priority options (third argument) so save stats runs first and audit log runs last, with send email in between at the default priority.
questions.explain: Higher priorities run first and the default is 0, so give the stats handler a positive priority and the audit log a negative one.
questions.expected:
save stats
send email
audit log

questions.q: After the publish, loop over result.errors and print <handlerId> failed: <cause message> for each failure. Then print how many handlers succeeded.
questions.explain: Each entry of result.errors is an EventHandlerError: handlerId is the id you gave the handler, and cause is what it threw. A handler can throw anything, so check that the cause is an Error before reading its message. The other handlers still ran.
questions.expected:
send-email failed: mail server is down
send-push failed: push service timeout
succeeded: 1

questions.q: Create the bus with an onError hook that prints logged: <event type> for every handler failure, using context.event.type. The publisher here never reads the result.
questions.explain: onError sees every failure, even when nobody reads the result. In the Task API, log the error there with the logger so it is never lost.

questions.q: Add a middleware with bus.use that prints -> <type> before the handlers run and <- <type> after them. Remember to return the result of next().
questions.explain: The code before await next() runs on the way in, the code after it on the way out. If you forget to return the result, the bus cannot see what the handlers did.

questions.q: Add validateEventMiddleware to the bus with bus.use (priority 100) so every event whose payload has no numeric taskId is rejected before the handler runs.
questions.explain: The check returns false for a missing taskId and for the string "2", so those publishes are rejected with an EventMiddlewareError. Priority 100 makes it the outermost layer. The middleware option of createEventBus works the same way.

questions.q: Finish complete(userId, id). If the task does not exist or belongs to someone else, throw new Error("Task <id> not found") before publishing anything. Otherwise set done to true and publish task.completed with the payload { taskId, userId, title }.
questions.explain: Check ownership first, then change the data, then publish. Once an event is out, every handler trusts it, so Linus's attempt must never reach the bus.
questions.expected:
linus: Task 1 not found
email to ada: "Buy milk"
done: true
